summary: The rules that keep aircraft apart. SERA and the UK rules apply ICAO Annex 2, and the commander always has to avoid collisions. Head-on aircraft turn right, the overtaker keeps clear, and converging aircraft give way to less manoeuvrable types or to traffic on their right. Near aerodromes you follow the pattern and turn left, the lower or final aircraft has priority, and navigation lights show which way another aircraft is heading. Low flying rules set 1,000 ft over congested areas and 500 ft elsewhere, with defined exemptions. On international flights you must know the interception signals: rock your wings and follow, squawk 7700 and call on 121.50 MHz.
sections: SERA and the UK rules of the air
Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 of 26 September 2012, as amended, set common rules of the air and operational provisions for air navigation services across EU states
On 1 January 2021 the UK left EASA and the regulations in force passed into UK law as retained EU law, now called assimilated law (EU Withdrawal Act 2018)
SERA applies ICAO standards and recommended practices and harmonises the ICAO airspace classification, supporting a single EU sky
The Single European Sky helps states meet their 1944 Chicago Convention obligations through a common interpretation and implementation
Only differences agreed by EU states are notified to ICAO
ICAO Annex 2 sets the international standards for the rules of the air; the UK and EU both fully endorse them
SERA applies to every aircraft in EU airspace, whatever its type or state of registry
SERA does not cover every aspect, so states may keep supplementary rules
UK rules assimilated under Article 249 of the ANO sit in a separate Statutory Instrument, usually bound with the ANO in CAP 393
Many permissions and exemptions last only a short period, so check they are still valid on the CAA website (ORS4, Official Record Series 4)
Scope and departures from the rules
The rules apply to all aircraft in the UK (including near offshore installations, where low flying is concerned) and to all UK-registered aircraft wherever they are
SERA may be departed from as far as necessary to avoid immediate danger, or to comply with the law of the country the aircraft is in
A departure for safety reasons must be reported in writing to the competent authority within 10 days
Collision avoidance (SERA.3201)
A collision risk exists when another aircraft is at the same level or approaching, its range is decreasing and its relative bearing stays constant
Regardless of any ATC clearance, the commander must take all possible measures to avoid colliding with any other aircraft
Do not fly so close to another aircraft as to create a danger of collision
No formation flying unless the commanders have agreed
An aircraft that must give way avoids passing over, under or crossing ahead of the other, unless passing well clear
An aircraft with right of way maintains its heading and speed
A glider and its tug count as one aircraft under the command of the tug; aeroplanes and helicopters must give way to aircraft towing gliders
Right of way (SERA.3210)
Head-on: if there is danger of collision, each aircraft turns right
Overtaking: the aircraft being overtaken has right of way; the overtaker, whether climbing, descending or level, keeps out of the way by turning right
An overtaking situation can be taken as approaching within 70° of the other aircraft's centreline
Converging, by category: power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to airships, sailplanes and balloons; airships give way to sailplanes and balloons; sailplanes give way to balloons
Converging, same category at about the same altitude: the aircraft with the other on its right gives way
Power-driven aircraft give way to those towing other aircraft or objects such as banners
Flights near an aerodrome (SERA.3225)
Unless ATC authorises otherwise, conform to the pattern formed by other landing aircraft or keep clear of the airspace where it is formed
Make all turns to the left unless ground signals direct otherwise
If ATC approves a straight-in approach, the pilot normally reports long final at 8 nm and final at 4 nm from the runway
Order of landing and take-off (Rules 9 and 10)
An aircraft landing or on final approach has right of way over others in flight or on the surface
When two or more aircraft approach to land, the lower aircraft has right of way, but must not cut in front of or overtake one on final approach
If ATC sets a landing order, follow it. If another aircraft is making an emergency landing, give way, and at night do not land until given further instruction
Power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to sailplanes in all cases
Take off and land in the direction shown by ground signals or, without them, into wind, unless good aviation practice demands otherwise
Do not land on a runway that is not clear unless ATC authorises it. Land after is not a landing clearance: the decision is yours, based on whether separation is sufficient (never given at night)
Where take-offs and landings are not confined to a runway, leave clear on your left any aircraft which has landed, is landing or is about to take off (keep right of other aircraft)
When taxiing on a landing area, turn left once you are satisfied it will not interfere with other traffic
A flying machine about to take off leaves clear on its left any aircraft which has taken off or is about to
After landing, move clear of the landing area as soon as possible unless ATC authorises otherwise
Radio in the ATZ and the right-hand traffic rule
In an Aerodrome Traffic Zone (ATZ), maintain appropriate radio or other communication with the aerodrome authority (ATC, Aerodrome Flight Information Service or Air/Ground Radio)
Before SERA, an aircraft following a road, railway, canal, coast or other line feature in sight of the ground had to keep it on its left, except in controlled airspace or when told otherwise
This is no longer a legal requirement, but the CAA strongly recommends it to keep separation from aircraft flying the opposite way along the same feature
Lights on aircraft (Rule 14, SERA.3215)

Aircraft must show the lights specified for their category so others can judge position and heading at night; the requirements generally apply when moving on the ground, and no other lights may be shown that impair them
If any required light fails in flight and cannot be repaired or replaced at once, the aircraft must land as soon as it is safe, unless ATC authorises continuing (Rule 15)
Flying machines and airships: green navigation light on the right (starboard) wing, red on the left (port) wing, each showing 110° from dead ahead
The white tail light shows through 70° either side of dead astern
The anti-collision light is a flashing red light visible in all directions
Red out to your left means your paths will not cross (red to red = safe); red out to your right may mean a collision risk (red to green = unsafe)
Green is the reverse: green to green = safe, green to red = unsafe
Red and green both visible: the other aircraft is heading straight at you. White visible: it is flying away from you

Airships also show a white nose light through 110° either side of dead ahead; gliders show the basic flying machine lights or a steady red light in all directions; free balloons show a steady red light in all directions
In the UK, night runs from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise
Low flying prohibitions (SERA.3105 and .5005(f))
Minimum heights are set in both EASA SERA and UK SERA, with some differences

UK and EASA, congested areas: not below 1,000 ft above the highest fixed object within 600 m, and able to land clear without undue hazard to persons or property if an emergency arises. Being able to land clear is the pilot's responsibility, not ATC's
EASA: not below 500 ft above the ground or water, or 500 ft above the highest obstacle within 150 m of the aircraft
UK, day only: not closer than 500 ft to any person, vehicle, vessel or structure
UK, at night: not below 500 ft above the ground or water, or 500 ft above the highest obstacle within 150 m

Exempt from the 500 ft and congested area rules when landing or taking off by normal aviation practice; the UK also exempts practising approaches to land or checking navigation aids or procedures at an aerodrome (under EASA a state authority may grant that exemption)
Open-air assemblies

EASA: except for take-off or landing, or with permission, do not fly over an organised open-air assembly of persons below the higher of 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m, or a height that allows a landing without undue hazard if an emergency arises
UK: the same heights apply over assemblies of more than 1,000 persons, and flying lower needs written permission from the CAA

UK: do not land or take off within 1,000 m of an assembly of more than 1,000 persons, except at an aerodrome using CAA-notified procedures, or at another landing site using notified procedures and the organiser's written permission
Exceptions to the low flying prohibitions

Take-off and landing: exempt when flying by normal aviation practice to take off, land, practise approaches or check navigation aids or procedures at an aerodrome; exempt from the 500 ft rule when landing, taking off or air-taxiing
Captive balloons and kites: no low flying prohibitions apply
Special VFR and notified routes: exempt from the 1,000 ft rule, but landings under this exemption only at a licensed or government aerodrome unless the CAA gives written permission
Balloons and helicopters: a balloon landing because it is becalmed is exempt from the 1,000 ft rule; a helicopter over a congested area is exempt from the land-clear rule
Police air operator's certificate: exempt from the 500 ft rule, the 1,000 ft rule and the open-air assembly prohibitions
Flying displays, air races and contests: exempt from the 500 ft rule within 1,000 m horizontally of the gathering
Glider hill-soaring: exempt from the 500 ft rule
Picking up or dropping tow ropes, banners or similar at an aerodrome: exempt from the 500 ft rule

Manoeuvring helicopters: exempt from the 500 ft rule within a licensed or government aerodrome (or elsewhere with written CAA permission), but not closer than 60 m to persons, vessels, vehicles or structures outside the site
Other rules: hazards, aerobatics and instrument practice
Exempt from the 500 ft rule: dropping articles with CAA permission for public health or against weather conditions, or under a CAA aerial application certificate
The CAA prosecutes alleged low flying
Report hazardous flight conditions to ATC as soon as possible, with details that matter to other aircraft: severe windshear or turbulence, rapidly worsening visibility, an unserviceable runway

Aerobatics (Rule 4): not over a congested area (any city, town or settlement used for residential, industrial, commercial or recreational purposes); in controlled airspace only with the controlling authority's approval

Simulated instrument flight (SERA.3220): fully working dual controls and a qualified safety pilot in the other control seat. A student pilot cannot be the safety pilot. Carry a third person as observer if needed for an adequate lookout
Practice instrument approaches in VMC: inform ATC and carry a competent observer
Misuse of signals (Rule 18): use specified signals and markings only for their meaning; never make signals that could be confused with them, and use military signals only with lawful authority
Interception: what to do (AIP ENR 1.12)
On international flights carry the interception procedures; they are in AIP ENR 1.12. Interception may be for military necessity, public safety, or to stop flight over restricted or danger areas
Stay calm and follow the intercepting aircraft's visual signals and instructions precisely
Tell the ATS unit you are working, if possible
Call the interceptor or intercept control on 121.50 MHz, giving your callsign and the nature of your flight
Squawk 7700 unless the ATS unit tells you otherwise
If another source (for example ATC) contradicts the interceptor, ask for clarification at once but obey the interceptor's visual instructions
Avoid hand signals: they are easily misread
If you are ever intercepted abroad, report it to the CAA
Interception signals

"Follow me": interceptor rocks its wings from slightly above and ahead (normally on your left), then makes a slow level turn, normally left. You: rock your wings and follow immediately; at night also flash your navigation lights at irregular intervals
Too slow to keep up? The interceptor flies racetrack patterns and rocks its wings each time it passes you
"You may proceed": an abrupt break-away climbing turn of 90° or more without crossing your line of flight. You: rock your wings

"Land at this aerodrome": interceptor circles, lowers its gear and overflies the runway in the landing direction (steady landing lights at night). You: lower gear if possible, follow, and land if, after overflying the runway, you judge it safe
"Aerodrome is inadequate" (from you): raise gear if possible while passing over the runway between 1,000 ft and 2,000 ft above aerodrome level, and keep circling
"I cannot comply" (from you): switch all lights on and off at regular intervals, distinct from flashing lights
"I am in distress" (from you): switch all lights on and off at irregular intervals
The interceptor answers "cannot comply" and "distress" with an abrupt break-away climbing turn, meaning "understood"
Interception radio phrases and ground signals

Without a common language, use the standard phrases. From you: CALLSIGN (my callsign is), WILCO (will comply), CAN NOT (unable to comply), REPEAT, AM LOST (position unknown), MAYDAY, HIJACK, LAND (place) (I request to land at), DESCEND (I require descent)
From the interceptor: FOLLOW (follow me), YOU LAND (land at this aerodrome), PROCEED (you may proceed)

Warning from the ground: projectiles fired every 10 seconds, each bursting into red and green lights or stars, by day or night. You are in, or about to enter, a restricted, prohibited or danger area: take remedial action

sum.SERA and the UK rules of the air: SERA applies ICAO Annex 2 standards across the EU; since Brexit the UK applies them as assimilated law, with its own supplementary rules in the ANO and CAP 393.
sum.Scope and departures from the rules: The rules cover all aircraft in the UK and UK-registered aircraft anywhere; you may depart from them to avoid immediate danger, then report within 10 days.
sum.Collision avoidance (SERA.3201): The commander is always responsible for avoiding collisions; the aircraft giving way keeps well clear and the one with right of way holds course and speed.
sum.Right of way (SERA.3210): Head-on, both turn right; the overtaker keeps clear by turning right; when converging, give way to the less manoeuvrable category, or to the aircraft on your right.
sum.Flights near an aerodrome (SERA.3225): Follow or stay clear of the traffic pattern and turn left, unless told otherwise.
sum.Order of landing and take-off (Rules 9 a: The lower aircraft, or the one on final, has priority; land and take off into wind, and 'land after' is not a clearance.
sum.Radio in the ATZ and the right-hand traf: Keep radio contact in an ATZ; keeping line features on your left is now only a recommendation.
sum.Lights on aircraft (Rule 14, SERA.3215): Green on the right wing, red on the left, white at the tail, plus a red anti-collision light; a failed light means landing as soon as safe, and UK night starts 30 minutes after sunset.
1,000 ft over congested areas and 500 ft elsewhere, with different UK and EASA wording; being able to land clear is the pilot's job.
sum.Open-air assemblies: Stay above the 1,000 ft or land-clear height over assemblies, and keep take-off and landing 1,000 m away unless an approved procedure applies.
sum.Exceptions to the low flying prohibition: Take-off, landing, special VFR, displays, hill-soaring and similar activities have defined exemptions from the 500 ft and 1,000 ft rules.
sum.Other rules: hazards, aerobatics and ins: Report hazards to ATC at once, no aerobatics over congested areas, a qualified safety pilot for simulated IF and a competent observer for practice approaches.
sum.Interception: what to do (AIP ENR 1.12): Follow the interceptor, call on 121.50 MHz, squawk 7700, and obey its visual signals over any conflicting instruction.
sum.Interception signals: Rock your wings to say understood; regular light flashing means cannot comply, irregular means distress.
sum.Interception radio phrases and ground si: Short standard phrases (WILCO, CAN NOT, AM LOST) when there is no common language; red and green stars every 10 seconds warn you off a restricted area.

cards.q: Which regulation introduced SERA, and when?
cards.a: Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 of 26 September 2012, as amended.

cards.q: What happened to EASA rules in the UK on 1 January 2021?
cards.a: They passed into UK law as retained EU law, now called assimilated law.

cards.q: Which ICAO Annex sets the international rules of the air?
cards.a: Annex 2.

cards.q: Where are the UK-assimilated rules of the air found?
cards.a: Under Article 249 of the ANO, in a separate Statutory Instrument usually bound with the ANO as CAP 393.

cards.q: Where do you check that a permission or exemption is still valid?
cards.a: The CAA website, ORS4 (Official Record Series 4).

cards.q: Which aircraft do the UK rules of the air apply to?
cards.a: All aircraft in the UK, and all UK-registered aircraft wherever they are.

cards.q: When may you depart from the rules of the air?
cards.a: As far as necessary to avoid immediate danger, or to comply with the law of the country you are in.

cards.q: How soon must a safety departure from the rules be reported?
cards.a: In writing to the competent authority within 10 days.

cards.q: When does a collision risk exist?
cards.a: Another aircraft is at the same level or approaching, its range is decreasing and its relative bearing stays constant.

cards.q: Who must avoid collisions, whatever ATC has cleared?
cards.a: The commander (pilot in command).

cards.q: What should an aircraft with right of way do?
cards.a: Maintain its heading and speed.

cards.q: How are a glider and its tug treated?
cards.a: As one aircraft under the command of the tug. Aeroplanes and helicopters give way to aircraft towing gliders.

cards.q: Head-on with a risk of collision: what does each aircraft do?
cards.a: Turn right.
cards.m: Everyone turns right in the air.

cards.q: Overtaking: who has right of way, and what does the overtaker do?
cards.a: The aircraft being overtaken. The overtaker keeps clear by turning right.

cards.q: What counts as an overtaking situation?
cards.a: Approaching from within 70° of the other aircraft's centreline.

cards.q: Converging: who gives way, by category?
cards.a: Power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to airships, sailplanes and balloons; airships to sailplanes and balloons; sailplanes to balloons.

cards.q: Converging in the same category at about the same altitude: who gives way?
cards.a: The aircraft that has the other on its right.

cards.q: Near an aerodrome, which way do you turn?
cards.a: Left, unless ground signals direct otherwise.

cards.q: On a straight-in approach, where are 'long final' and 'final' reported?
cards.a: Long final at 8 nm, final at 4 nm from the runway.
cards.m: 8 then 4: long final is twice final.

cards.q: Two aircraft approach to land: who has priority?
cards.a: The lower aircraft, but it must not cut in front of or overtake one on final. An aircraft on final has right of way over others.

cards.q: What does ATC's 'land after' mean?
cards.a: It is not a clearance to land. You decide whether separation is sufficient. It is never given at night.
cards.m: Land after is a heads-up, never a clearance.

cards.q: Is the right-hand traffic rule still a legal requirement?
cards.a: No. Keeping a line feature on your left is only strongly recommended by the CAA.

cards.q: Which colour navigation light is on which wing?
cards.a: Green on the right (starboard) wing, red on the left (port) wing, each showing 110° from dead ahead.
cards.m: Port wine is red: port is left, so red is on the left wing.

cards.q: How much of the sky does the white tail light cover?
cards.a: 70° either side of dead astern.

cards.q: Red to red, green to green: safe or unsafe?
cards.a: Safe. Red to green and green to red are unsafe.
cards.m: Red to red, green to green: safe to go on. Mixed colours means take care.

cards.q: You see both red and green lights on another aircraft. What does it mean?
cards.a: It is heading straight at you. A white light means it is flying away.

cards.q: What must you do if a required light fails in flight?
cards.a: Land as soon as it is safe, unless ATC authorises continuing.

cards.q: When does night start and end in the UK?
cards.a: From 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise.

cards.q: Minimum height over a congested area?
cards.a: 1,000 ft above the highest fixed object within 600 m, and able to land clear in an emergency. Landing clear is the pilot's responsibility.

cards.q: UK 500 ft rule by day?
cards.a: Not closer than 500 ft to any person, vehicle, vessel or structure.

cards.q: EASA 500 ft rule?
cards.a: Not below 500 ft above the ground or water, or 500 ft above the highest obstacle within 150 m.

cards.q: How close may you take off or land to an open-air assembly of more than 1,000 persons?
cards.a: Not within 1,000 m, except at an aerodrome using CAA procedures or at an approved site with the organiser's written permission.

cards.q: Do the low flying prohibitions apply to captive balloons and kites?
cards.a: No.

cards.q: How close may a manoeuvring helicopter under the exemption get to people and property outside the site?
cards.a: Not closer than 60 m.

cards.q: Which low flying exemption covers crop spraying and similar work?
cards.a: Dropping articles with CAA permission, or under a CAA aerial application certificate (exempt from the 500 ft rule).

cards.q: Which hazardous conditions must you report to ATC, and when?
cards.a: As soon as possible: things like severe windshear or turbulence, rapidly worsening visibility, or an unserviceable runway.

cards.q: Where may you not fly aerobatics?
cards.a: Over a congested area. In controlled airspace only with the controlling authority's approval.

cards.q: What do you need for simulated instrument flight?
cards.a: Working dual controls and a qualified safety pilot in the other control seat (not a student pilot), plus an observer if needed for lookout.

cards.q: Practising instrument approaches in VMC: what two things are required?
cards.a: Inform ATC and carry a competent observer.

cards.q: Where are the interception procedures published?
cards.a: AIP ENR 1.12.

cards.q: Intercepted: which frequency and which squawk?
cards.a: Call on 121.50 MHz with your callsign and nature of flight; squawk 7700 unless the ATS unit says otherwise.

cards.q: ATC and the interceptor give conflicting instructions. What do you do?
cards.a: Ask for clarification at once, but obey the interceptor's visual instructions.

cards.q: Interceptor rocks its wings from ahead, then turns slowly left. Meaning and your reply?
cards.a: "Follow me." Rock your wings and follow immediately (at night, also flash navigation lights at irregular intervals).

cards.q: Interceptor makes an abrupt climbing turn of 90° or more without crossing your path. Meaning?
cards.a: "You may proceed." Reply by rocking your wings.

cards.q: Interceptor lowers its gear and overflies the runway. Meaning and reply?
cards.a: "Land at this aerodrome." Lower gear if possible, follow, and land if it looks safe.

cards.q: How do you signal "this aerodrome is inadequate"?
cards.a: Raise gear (if possible) while passing over the runway between 1,000 and 2,000 ft above aerodrome level, and keep circling.

cards.q: Lights switched on and off at regular vs irregular intervals?
cards.a: Regular = I cannot comply. Irregular = I am in distress.

cards.q: What do WILCO, CAN NOT and AM LOST mean in interception phrases?
cards.a: Will comply; unable to comply; position unknown.

cards.q: Red and green stars fired from the ground every 10 seconds?
cards.a: You are in, or about to enter, a restricted, prohibited or danger area. Take remedial action.

cards.q: Night, steady relative bearing of 330°, you see the other aircraft's green light. What now?
cards.a: Collision risk (green to red). It has you on its right so it must give way: you hold heading and speed.

quiz.q: Which ICAO Annex sets the international standards for the rules of the air?
quiz.why: Annex 2. Annex 1 covers licensing, Annex 11 air traffic services and Annex 15 aeronautical information services.

quiz.q: Which CAA publication usually binds the ANO with the assimilated rules of the air?
quiz.why: CAP 393. CAP 413 is the radiotelephony guide, CAP 637 the visual aids handbook and CAP 1535 the Skyway Code.

quiz.q: Within how many days must a safety departure from the rules be reported in writing?
quiz.why: Ten days, to the competent authority.

quiz.q: Two aircraft approach head-on with a danger of collision. What does each do?
quiz.why: Each turns right.

quiz.q: An aircraft is being overtaken. Who has right of way?
quiz.why: The aircraft being overtaken. The overtaker keeps clear by turning right.

quiz.q: Two aeroplanes converge at about the same altitude. Who gives way?
o: The one with the other on its left
The one with the other on its right
quiz.why: The aircraft that has the other on its right gives way.

quiz.q: A power-driven aeroplane converges with a balloon. Who gives way?
quiz.why: Power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to airships, sailplanes and balloons.

quiz.q: Within what angle of the other aircraft's centreline is an approach treated as overtaking?
quiz.why: Within 70° of the overtaken aircraft's centreline.

quiz.q: Which way do you turn near an aerodrome, unless told otherwise?
quiz.why: Left, unless ground signals direct otherwise.

quiz.q: Where is 'long final' reported on a straight-in approach?
quiz.why: Long final at 8 nm, final at 4 nm.

quiz.q: ATC says 'land after'. What does this mean?
o: You decide whether separation is sufficient
quiz.why: It is not a landing clearance. The decision is yours, based on whether you judge separation sufficient.

quiz.q: Which main navigation light is on the left (port) wing?
quiz.why: Red on the left, green on the right.

quiz.q: Through what angle does the white tail light show?
quiz.why: 70° either side of dead astern. The red and green lights show 110° from dead ahead.

quiz.q: You see an approaching aircraft's red light out to your left. What does this suggest?
quiz.why: Red to red is safe. Red to green is unsafe.

quiz.q: A required light fails in flight and cannot be repaired. What must you do?
o: Land as soon as it is safe, unless ATC authorises continuing
quiz.why: Rule 15: land as soon as it is safe unless ATC authorises you to continue.

quiz.q: When does night begin in the UK?
o: At the end of civil twilight
quiz.why: Night runs from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise.

quiz.q: What is the minimum height over a congested area?
o: 500 ft above the highest obstacle within 150 m
1,000 ft above the highest fixed object within 600 m
quiz.why: 1,000 ft above the highest fixed object within 600 m, and you must be able to land clear in an emergency.

quiz.q: Who is responsible for being able to land clear over a congested area?
quiz.why: The pilot, not ATC.

quiz.q: What is the UK daytime 500 ft rule?
o: Not below 500 ft above the ground
Not closer than 500 ft to any person, vehicle, vessel or structure
Not within 500 ft of an aerodrome
quiz.why: By day, not closer than 500 ft to any person, vehicle, vessel or structure.

quiz.q: How close may you take off or land to an open-air assembly of more than 1,000 persons, outside an approved procedure?
quiz.why: Not within 1,000 m, except at an aerodrome using CAA procedures or an approved site with written permission.

quiz.q: Which of these is exempt from the low flying prohibitions?
quiz.why: No low flying prohibitions apply to captive balloons and kites. Gliders are exempt only when hill-soaring, and only from the 500 ft rule.

quiz.q: How close may a manoeuvring helicopter under the exemption get to people outside the site?
quiz.why: Not closer than 60 m to persons, vessels, vehicles or structures outside the aerodrome or site.

quiz.q: Who is ultimately responsible for taking every possible measure to avoid a collision?
o: The most qualified pilot on board
quiz.why: The commander (pilot in command), whatever clearance ATC has given. ATC and A/G can help but the duty stays with the commander.

quiz.q: When converging, what must the aircraft with right of way do?
quiz.why: SERA says heading (course) and speed. Height is not mentioned, which is the usual trap.

quiz.q: What is the minimum height over a congested area of a city, town or settlement?
o: 300 m (1,000 ft) above the highest obstacle within 300 m
300 m (1,000 ft) above the highest obstacle within 600 m
600 m (2,000 ft) above the highest obstacle within 600 m
150 m (500 ft) above the highest obstacle within 150 m
quiz.why: 1,000 ft (300 m) above the highest obstacle within 600 m, and high enough to land clear. 500 ft within 150 m is the rule elsewhere.

quiz.q: Two aircraft approach to land at the same place. Neither has an emergency and ATC has set no order. Who has priority?
o: The aircraft closest to the threshold
The lower aircraft, but it must not cut in front of or overtake one on final
quiz.why: The lower aircraft, with the caveat that it must not cut in front of or overtake an aircraft on final. The plain 'lower aircraft' option misses that caveat.

quiz.q: Which right-of-way order for converging aircraft is correct?
o: Balloons give way to airships and sailplanes
Sailplanes give way to power-driven aircraft, airships and balloons
Power-driven aircraft give way to airships, sailplanes and balloons
Airships give way to power-driven aircraft, sailplanes and balloons
quiz.why: The least manoeuvrable has priority: power-driven aircraft give way to airships, sailplanes and balloons; airships to sailplanes and balloons; sailplanes to balloons.

quiz.q: At night you see another aircraft's green light on a steady relative bearing of 330°, at a similar level. What should you do?
o: Collision risk: hold your heading and speed
quiz.why: 330° is at your 11 o'clock. Its green light faces your red wing (green to red = unsafe) and the bearing is steady, so there is a risk. It has you on its right, so it gives way: you keep heading and speed.

quiz.q: At night you see another aircraft's red light on a steady relative bearing of 030°, at a similar level. What should you do?
o: No action: red means it is moving away
Collision risk: hold heading and speed
Collision risk: you give way, normally by turning right to pass behind it
quiz.why: It is at your 1 o'clock showing red (red to green = unsafe). It is on your right, so you give way, avoiding passing ahead of it. A right turn takes you behind it.

quiz.q: At night you see only a steady white light ahead of you, getting closer at your level. What is happening?
o: It is heading straight at you
You are overtaking it, so you must keep clear by turning right
It is a balloon, which has right of way
quiz.why: A white light alone is the tail light, so it is flying away from you. If it is getting closer you are the overtaker: keep clear and turn right.

quiz.q: At night you see both the red and the green light of another aircraft, dead ahead at your level. What do you do?
quiz.why: Seeing both wing lights means it is heading straight at you. Head-on: both aircraft turn right.

quiz.q: You are flying an aeroplane and converging with a tug that is towing a glider. Who gives way?
o: The tug, because it is power-driven
You, because aircraft towing gliders have priority
quiz.why: A glider and its tug count as one aircraft. Aeroplanes and helicopters give way to aircraft towing gliders, banners or other objects.

quiz.q: A helicopter and an aeroplane converge at about the same altitude, with the aeroplane on the helicopter's right. Who gives way?
o: The aeroplane, because helicopters are more manoeuvrable
quiz.why: Both are power-driven heavier-than-air, so the same-category rule applies: the aircraft with the other on its right gives way.

quiz.q: An aircraft is landing on final, and you are lower but on base leg. What should you do?
o: Turn final ahead of it, as the lower aircraft
Let it land first; do not cut in front of an aircraft on final
quiz.why: The lower aircraft normally has priority, but must never cut in front of or overtake one on final approach.

quiz.q: Who may act as the safety pilot during simulated instrument flight?
o: Any passenger with a good view
A student pilot with at least 20 hours
A qualified pilot in a control seat with working dual controls
quiz.why: SERA.3220 needs fully working dual controls and a qualified safety pilot in the other control seat. A student pilot cannot do it.

quiz.q: You want to practise an instrument approach in VMC, without screens. What is required?
o: Inform ATC and carry a competent observer
quiz.why: Inform ATC and carry a competent observer.

quiz.q: Where may aerobatics not be flown?
quiz.why: Not over a congested area. In controlled airspace you need the controlling authority's approval.

quiz.q: You meet severe windshear on approach. What must you do?
o: Note it in the tech log after landing
Report it to ATC as soon as possible
Report it to the CAA within 10 days
quiz.why: Report hazardous conditions to ATC as soon as possible so they can warn others.

quiz.q: You are being intercepted. Which squawk do you select?
quiz.why: 7700, unless the ATS unit tells you otherwise. 7500 is unlawful interference and 7600 radio failure.

quiz.q: On which frequency do you try to contact the intercepting aircraft?
quiz.why: 121.50 MHz, giving your callsign and the nature of your flight.

quiz.q: The interceptor rocks its wings from slightly above and ahead, then makes a slow level turn to the left. What does it mean, and how do you reply?
o: You may proceed; rock your wings
Follow me; rock your wings and follow
You are in distress; flash your lights
quiz.why: That is "follow me". Rock your wings and follow immediately (at night, also flash your navigation lights at irregular intervals).

quiz.q: The interceptor makes an abrupt break-away climbing turn of 90° or more without crossing your flight path. What does it mean?
quiz.why: You may proceed. Rock your wings to acknowledge.

quiz.q: The interceptor circles an aerodrome, lowers its gear and overflies the runway. What should you do?
o: Lower your gear if possible, follow it and land if it looks safe
quiz.why: It means "land at this aerodrome". Lower your gear, follow, and land if, after overflying the runway, you judge it safe.

quiz.q: How do you tell an interceptor that the aerodrome it has chosen is inadequate?
o: Flash all lights at irregular intervals
Raise your gear while passing over the runway between 1,000 and 2,000 ft above aerodrome level, and keep circling
quiz.why: Raise gear (if possible) over the runway between 1,000 and 2,000 ft above aerodrome level and keep circling. Avoid hand signals.

quiz.q: You switch all your lights on and off at regular intervals. What are you telling the interceptor?
quiz.why: Regular = cannot comply. Irregular = distress.

quiz.q: ATC tells you to turn right, but the intercepting aircraft is signalling you to follow it left. What do you do?
o: Follow ATC, since you are on their frequency
Follow the interceptor's visual instructions and ask for clarification
Hold your heading until it is resolved
quiz.why: Request clarification at once, but obey the interceptor's visual instructions.

quiz.q: In the interception phrases, what does "CAN NOT" mean?
quiz.why: CAN NOT = unable to comply. REPEAT, AM LOST and DESCEND are the others.

quiz.q: By day you see projectiles fired from the ground every 10 seconds, bursting into red and green stars. What does it mean?
o: You are in or about to enter a restricted, prohibited or danger area
quiz.why: It warns an unauthorised aircraft that it is in, or about to enter, a restricted, prohibited or danger area. Take remedial action.

quiz.q: Where are the interception procedures you must carry on international flights published?
quiz.why: AIP ENR 1.12. GEN 1.7 lists UK differences from ICAO.
